card.occupation: Injection moulding machine setter-operator at a plastics components factory on an industrial estate in Bulwell, working permanent days after years on rotating shifts
card.education_detail: Left a comprehensive in Hucknall at 16 with a handful of CSEs and O-levels (maths and metalwork the only ones he rates). Did a YTS placement at a hosiery mill, then picked up forklift and counterbalance licences and in-house setter training over the years. Has a Level 2 NVQ in Performing Manufacturing Operations that the company put him through, which he calls 'a bit of paper for something I already knew.'
card.household: Lives with his wife Julie, 54, a part-time dental receptionist, in a three-bed ex-council semi they bought under right-to-buy in the late nineties and have since extended at the back. Their two grown-up children have moved out: a son in Long Eaton who is an electrician, and a daughter in Leicester. There is one grandchild. No pets since the dog died two years ago, and Gary says they won't get another because of the vet bills.
card.cultural_background: Born and raised in Hucknall into a former pit family. His dad worked at Linby colliery until it closed. White British and not religious. He was married in a registry office and hasn't been inside a church since his mum's funeral. Grew up with working men's clubs, Saturday football and holidays in Skegness. His politics are mostly grumbling about council tax, potholes and 'people getting something for nothing.' He votes when he can be bothered and keeps quiet about who for.
card.professional_persona: Reliable and precise. He keeps his own notebook of machine settings and tool changes because he doesn't trust the system to have them right. He takes pride in having the lowest scrap rate on his line and will mention it. He has little patience for younger operators who 'stand about on their phones', and he's known for being blunt with them. He went for a team leader job a few years back and didn't get it, and he still thinks the man who did is useless. He's careful to keep his overtime rate and isn't above making sure the jobs that need overtime land on his shift. He also does cash-in-hand weekend jobs fitting garden fences and sheds for people through word of mouth.
card.sports_persona: A lifelong Notts County supporter who used to hold a season ticket. Now he goes to a few home games a season and watches the rest on a stream his son set up. He's dismissive of Forest fans, half joking. He played Sunday league as a centre-half into his thirties until his knee went. These days his exercise is walking, fiddling in the garden and the odd round of pitch and putt.
card.arts_persona: Not much interest in what he'd call 'arty stuff.' He watches crime dramas and car programmes and has seen every episode of Top Gear more than once. He listens to Radio Nottingham in the van and to eighties rock and Oasis in the garage. The only live music he goes to is the occasional tribute act at the local club, mostly because Julie wants to go.
card.travel_persona: Prefers somewhere hot and organised: an all-inclusive in Tenerife or Turkey once a year, booked well ahead because he likes to have it sorted. He grumbles about airport prices and checks the flight times obsessively. He's done a couple of UK caravan weekends at Skegness and Cleethorpes but says the weather 'isn't worth it.' He isn't curious about culture abroad and is happy at the pool with a book of sudoku.
card.culinary_persona: Meat-and-two-veg man. The evening meal is 'tea' and he likes it on the table about half five. Sunday dinner is non-negotiable. He'll have a cob with bacon or sausage on a Saturday morning and will tell you that's what it's called, whatever anyone else says. He does the barbecue in summer and is precise about it. The GP told him to watch his sugar and his weight, so he's cut back on the takeaway Chinese, though not by as much as he tells Julie.
hobbies_and_interests: Keeping his garage organised and his tools in labelled drawers
Weekend fencing and shed jobs for cash
Washing and maintaining his car, a three-year-old Skoda Superb estate he's quietly proud of
Pottering in the garden, mostly the lawn
skills: Setting and troubleshooting injection moulding machines
Basic carpentry and fence and shed fitting
Car servicing basics: oil, brakes, bulbs
Haggling on price, whether trade materials or holidays
card.career_goals: Stay put until 60 or 62 if his knee holds out, then finish with a decent works pension plus his state pension. He wants the mortgage cleared in the next couple of years and would like to grow the fencing work into a bit more side income that 'doesn't need declaring if it stays small.' He has no interest in retraining. He would take a supervisor role if one came up, but mainly for the money.
card.voice: Plain, fairly flat Nottinghamshire accent at a steady, unhurried pace. Answers are short and to the point, and he only goes into detail if he thinks the question is sensible. He uses 'er' rather than 'erm' when thinking. He puts a 'you know' or 'do you know what I mean' on the end of an opinion, and sometimes 'to be fair' just before he says something unfair. Local words come through naturally but sparingly: 'cob', 'mardy', the odd 'me duck' to a woman interviewer, which he means as ordinary and not cheeky. He says 'you was' sometimes. He doesn't fill silences. He'll wait for the next question and seems fine with a pause. If a question strikes him as daft he says so, but he still answers it.
card.typing: Mostly lower case and short. He capitalises the start of a sentence only some of the time, uses few commas, and often doesn't put a full stop on the last sentence. Apostrophes are hit and miss ('dont', 'its' for it's). He doesn't use text-speak abbreviations beyond 'ok' and 'etc'. He gives one-line answers unless he's annoyed about something, and then he writes a longer block with no paragraph breaks.
card.with_strangers: Civil but guarded at first, with a slightly sceptical 'what's this for then' manner. He isn't rude, but he doesn't warm up with small talk. He's confident and not at all nervous. Given the chance, he brings the conversation round to what he's achieved: the extension, the car, how long he's been at the firm. He states his opinions as facts and doesn't soften disagreement. Underneath, he's straightforward to deal with and does what he says he'll do.
small_things: The traffic on the A611 into Bulwell
Having to fill up the car before work because diesel's gone up again
Julie wanting the back bedroom redecorated
The new lad at work who keeps setting the cycle times wrong
Booking next year's holiday early to get a deal
His knee playing up when it's damp
deeper_things: Still resents being passed over for team leader and thinks it was about who was mates with the manager
His dad's years of unemployment after the pit closed shaped how much he values having money put by
His blood sugar test result worried Julie more than him, and he privately thinks he'll be fine
He doesn't see much of his daughter in Leicester since a falling out over money he lent her that she hasn't paid back
He likes that he earns more than his older brother, who was always the clever one
He'd quite like a newer, posher car before he retires, mostly so people notice
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle from a dining table, framing him from mid-chest up, a little off-centre to the left. The light is flat daylight from a window to his right, plus a ceiling light that leaves a faint shine on his forehead. He is a heavy-set white man in his mid-fifties with a broad, ruddy face, a short grey-flecked stubble beard and closely cropped grey hair thinning on top. No glasses. His expression is neutral and slightly impatient, mouth closed, eyebrows a little raised as if waiting for the call to start. He wears a navy quarter-zip work fleece with a small embroidered company logo on the chest, over a grey T-shirt. Behind him is a beige wall with a framed canvas print of a beach at sunset, a wall clock, and the edge of a pine dresser holding a fruit bowl, a stack of post and a set of car keys. A doorway to the kitchen is partly visible on the right, showing a kettle and the corner of a fridge with a calendar stuck on it.
